reading.body:
At 3.75 MW of published IT capacity, this campus is the smallest among the fifteen Texas facilities on this site that have published a megawatt figure. Assuming 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 3.75 MW supports roughly 94 racks, and the arithmetic changes significantly at higher densities, for example 80 kW per rack yields about 47 racks. The 100,807 square feet of technical space is large relative to that power figure, which suggests the floor plan was designed for lower-density, higher-footprint deployments rather than tightly packed GPU clusters. The campus contributes less than one percent of the 399.41 MW published across all fifteen Texas sites this site has read.

The six certifications on file qualify this campus to host specific categories of regulated workload. SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 qualify it for financial and operational controls audits. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment card data. ITAR qualifies it for controlled defense and export-restricted information. HITRUST qualifies it for healthcare data under HIPAA-aligned frameworks. SSAE 18 is the auditing standard under which the SOC reports are issued. No tenants are published.

Texas hosts 133 mapped data center facilities in this site's records, of which only 15 have published a megawatt figure, so the state's true capacity is almost certainly larger than 399.41 MW. Richardson sits within the Dallas-Fort Worth metro, which concentrates most of the state's data center activity, but the grid constraints and interconnection timelines that apply to larger Texas campuses are not published for this site, so no judgment about power availability here can be drawn from the data on hand. For AI workloads that require regulated data handling at modest scale, the certification stack is the relevant qualification; for raw training capacity, 3.75 MW is not a meaningful number at the state level.
